lesson.title: Vanishing Packets: Why Loss Happens and What It Costs You
lesson.summary: Packet loss happens when a sent packet never arrives, most often because a congested router's buffer overflowed, and how badly it hurts depends on which transport protocol is carrying the data.
lesson.body:
Packet loss is exactly what it sounds like: a packet that was sent by the source never arrives at its destination. Every packet is a discrete, self contained unit of data, and loss means that particular unit simply disappears somewhere along the path rather than showing up late. Loss is usually reported as a percentage, the fraction of packets sent that never arrived, over some window of time or some number of packets.

There are a few distinct reasons a packet can be lost. The most common cause on congested networks is a full buffer: when a router's outbound queue is already packed with waiting packets and a new one arrives, there is nowhere to put it, so the router simply discards it, a behavior known as tail drop. This connects directly to queuing delay from earlier in this sequence, since a queue only fills up in the first place because packets are arriving faster than the link can transmit them. Other causes include bit errors on physically noisy links such as wireless connections, where corrupted packets get discarded because a checksum fails, hardware or link failures that make a path temporarily unreachable, and a packet's time to live counter reaching zero because it looped through too many routers.

Suppose a VoIP call sends 1,000 packets over its duration and 15 of them never arrive. The loss rate is 15 divided by 1,000, or 1.5 percent. Voice codecs generally include some loss concealment, techniques that mask a missing chunk of audio by interpolating from surrounding packets, so a loss rate under about 1 percent is often barely noticeable to a listener. Once loss climbs past 1 to 2 percent, most people start to hear the audio degrade, with occasional dropouts or robotic sounding artifacts, which is why network operators treat sustained loss above roughly that range as a real quality problem for real time traffic.

How an application responds to packet loss depends heavily on which transport protocol it uses. TCP treats a lost packet as a strong signal of network congestion. It detects the loss, retransmits the missing data, and deliberately reduces how fast it sends afterward, on the theory that the network told it to slow down. UDP does none of this. It has no built in retransmission or loss detection at all, so if an application needs guaranteed delivery on top of UDP, it has to build that logic itself, and if it does not, as is common for live voice and video where a late retransmission would be useless anyway, lost data is simply gone.

Because tail drop from full buffers is such a common cause of loss, many routers use active queue management techniques, such as randomly dropping or marking a small number of packets before a queue completely fills, as an early warning to senders to slow down before the buffer overflows and causes a burst of loss all at once. Packet loss and packet size are also connected through the maximum transmission unit, covered next, since a packet that is too large for a link to carry can be discarded outright if fragmentation is not permitted.
